Nos apasiona ver cómo podemos crear grandes soluciones para problemas cotidianos y, por qué no, aplicar esto también al sector espacial. ¡Así que no dudes en escribirnos!
summary:
Our project is a geospatial analysis platform designed to identify locations on Earth where processes relevant to future lunar bases and Mars exploration can be studied. It supports the selection of sites for research, training, and technology testing.

The project integrates publicly available NASA and USGS data into a database containing more than 58 million records.

Its comparison engine currently uses four terrain properties: mean slope, slope variability, roughness, and local relief.

Additional information on surface temperature, aridity, permafrost, wind, dust, materials, and geological formations helps characterize the context of each location.

Through an interactive 3D viewer, users can explore candidate Earth analogs associated with nine lunar regions and twelve Martian sites, review ranked results, apply filters, and examine documented caves and lava tubes. Each comparison explains how the terrains match and which differences must be considered, including the gravity, pressure, and atmospheric conditions of each celestial body.

Its main contribution is transforming large volumes of geoscientific data into clear, verifiable comparisons.
details:
ExoTwins is a geospatial analysis platform developed by our team

Its purpose is to identify and characterize locations on Earth that can help researchers study processes relevant to future lunar bases and Mars exploration. We want to help scientists, engineers, educators, and exploration teams select environments for field research, training, instrument testing, and technology demonstrations.

The project connects planetary science with Earth observation data. A terrestrial location can reproduce some useful characteristics of a lunar or Martian environment while differing substantially in others. Our platform makes those relationships explicit so users can understand both the value and the limitations of each proposed analog.

We built the system around three connected stages:

  1. Data preparation. Our Python ETL pipeline processes geospatial datasets and organizes their measurements using a common HEALPix spatial index. The current master dataset contains 58,700,374 terrestrial grid cells and 80 source columns. It includes information about terrain, surface temperature, vegetation, aridity, permafrost, wind, dust, surface materials, and geological features. Sources include NASA, USGS, Copernicus, and other scientific data providers.
  2. Scientific comparison. Our Rust search engine compares eligible Earth cells with nine lunar regions and twelve Martian sites. The current validated ranking uses four terrain properties: mean slope, slope variability, roughness, and local relief. These measurements are evaluated at comparable analysis scales, with normalization and correlation handling to support comparisons between quantities with different units and relationships. Environmental layers provide additional context and filtering capabilities. A similarity score describes the selected terrain profile; its interpretation also requires considering planetary conditions and data limitations.
  3. Interactive exploration. The engine produces compact files for a browser-based 3D viewer. Users can explore ranked candidates, inspect their measurements, apply environmental filters, and examine documented caves and lava tubes. The current results contain 200 candidates per target, producing 4,200 candidate entries across the 21 searches. The same location may be relevant to multiple targets. Our cave layer currently includes a curated, partial catalogue of 57 verified entrances representing 55 systems.

The platform’s practical benefit is that it brings a complex screening process into a form that people can inspect and discuss. Users can examine the measurements supporting a match, compare them with the planetary target, review sources, and identify missing information. This can support shortlisting locations for rover exercises, geological fieldwork, equipment trials, or training activities before more detailed investigation.

Our intended impact is to make terrestrial analog research more systematic and accessible. A global search framework can help researchers investigate less familiar locations and formulate new hypotheses about environments worth studying. It can also support education by showing how observations of Earth contribute to understanding other worlds. These are intended applications; selecting an operational test site still requires expert assessment and field verification.

The development combined several technologies:

Technology

Role in the project

Python and NumPy

ETL processing, numerical calculations, data checks, and independent validation.

GDAL, Astropy, pyproj, and cdshealpix

Reading scientific formats, transforming coordinates, and working with spatial grids.

PyArrow and Parquet

Reading and reconstructing reference datasets used in validation.

Rust, Rayon, and memory-mapped files

Efficient searches across large numerical datasets with controlled parallel processing.

TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS

Viewer behavior, interfaces, data loading, and presentation.

CesiumJS

Interactive Earth, Moon, and Mars visualization.

Vite and Node.js

Frontend development, builds, testing, and integration tooling.

Git, GitHub, and Pixi

Collaboration, version control, automated checks, and reproducible environments.

PostgreSQL

Local data-loading and cave-integration workflows. The current validated viewer consumes precomputed files.

Large datasets are processed offline, and the browser receives lightweight derivatives. AI-assisted development tools also supported programming, debugging, review, and documentation; numerical results were produced through defined processing routines and checked against data.

The project’s creativity lies in combining a global spatial framework, interpretable statistical comparisons, planetary context, and interactive visualization. It treats an analog as a relationship between measurable characteristics and processes. Bringing cave information into the same exploration interface also broadens the investigation to documented subsurface environments.

Several factors shaped our design:

  • Scientific comparability: Measurements must have compatible definitions, units, and analysis scales.
  • Planetary differences: Gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, and environmental conditions affect how an Earth analog can be used.
  • Coverage and missing data: Gaps remain visible, and measurements retain their source-resolution limitations.
  • Reproducibility: Input hashes, recorded parameters, audit trails, and independent numerical checks make results reviewable.
  • Computational resources: Offline processing and compact web outputs help make a large dataset usable on local hardware.
  • Usability: Maps, ranked results, comparisons, and visible limitations help users understand the evidence.

Our goal is to provide an explainable starting point for exploration planning: a way to discover promising terrestrial environments, understand their relevance, and determine what further investigation is needed.
